CONGRESS AND THE LAWMAKING PROCESS
arrangements, task forces, leadership-organized panels, outside 
blue-ribbon commissions, and “high level summit’ conferences be­
tween legislative leaders and the executive branch.”^^ From time to 
time, in the effort to strengthen its institutional capacity to perform 
its role as a coequal branch of government,^ Congress will examine 
and make changes in its operations; one such effort I recall first­
hand, having testified before a joint committee on the organization 
of Congress.^
Congressional decisionmaking is the product of multiple deci­
sion points; it is the product of both centrifugal and centripetal 
forces. Tlie latter is characterized by the decentralization of the 
committee system, and the former by efforts towards centraliza­
tion, leadership at the top, and party discipline. Judge Coffin, a 
former legislator, once noted: “What complicates matters is that 
both movements coexist today, something hke the various shiftings 
of the tectonic plates underlying the continents.”^^ Many factors 
account for ambiguous or vague legislation: the difficulty of foresee­
ing all problems; the often inherent imprecisions of language itself; 
the legislature’s decision to identify an issue generally and then to 
delegate the issue to the executive branch for resolution; and the 
nature of coahtion politics which, in cobbling together the neces­
sary majority, may yield legislation that is dehberately vague and 
ambiguous. Congressional organization—with its many decision 
points—can firustrate coherent decisionmaking, producing muddy 
statutory language. And political polarization, partisanship, and 
gridlock further comphcate deliberation and the task of passing 
laws that are plainly understood.^®
Each chamber has its own rules of procedure for referring legisla­
tion to committees and calling up measures for floor consideration.
